ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: The Giant's Chain, And A Volcano Cut In Half

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: That stripe has a folk tale and a geology paper, and they describe **the same object.** The story says it is a **troll-woman's silver chain.** The geology says it is the **feeder pipe the volcano erupted through.** Both are correct.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: **Festarfjall** is a **stapi** — a tuya. It erupted underneath the ice sheet: móberg breccia below, a cap of grey basalt on top where the eruption finally broke the surface. About **190 metres.** And then the sea did something rare and generous — **it cut the mountain in half.** You are looking at a **cross-section of a volcano's internal plumbing**, which almost never gets exposed.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: The stripe is **Festin**, "the chain": a **basalt dyke**, and — per the geologist **Kristján Sæmundsson** — the **aðfærsluæð**, the conduit the magma actually came up. Harder than the rock around it, so as the sea grinds the cliff back, the dyke stands proud. The mountain is literally wearing its own throat on the outside.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: The tale is recorded in **Rauðskinna**, the folk-tale collection — *not* Jón Árnason, and guides get that wrong. A troll-woman hung a **silver chain** over the cliff and declared that when the farmer at **Hraun** had a daughter named after her, and that girl walked on the sand below, the chain would fall and be hers. **She then neglected to mention her own name.** So the chain is still up there. *(Worst-designed raffle in the North Atlantic.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: The farm ahead is **Ísólfsskáli**, documented from **1703** as a Skálholt property. Bishop **Brynjólfur Sveinsson** ran a fishing station from it, and in **1734** the Skálholt boat was lost here with **ten men.** The 1703 land register warned the well was so bad the farm might have to be abandoned for want of water. The **earthquakes of 28–29 January 1905** brought the kitchen down, the farm stood empty **three years**, and in **1916** they rebuilt it **further back from the sea.** For decades it was the **last farm on this whole peninsula living purely off farming.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Seltún → Fagradalsfjall / ⛓️ Festarfjall & Ísólfsskáli
en: One honest correction, because it gets repeated: **the eruptions of 2023 to 2025 did not reach Ísólfsskáli.** Those were all at the **Sundhnúkur crater row above Grindavík.** The drama on *this* road was **2021**, when lava came down into **Nátthagi** and civil protection bulldozed **eight-metre barriers** to keep it off **Suðurstrandarvegur** — because this road is **Grindavík's escape route** and it carries the peninsula's **fibre-optic cable.**

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: A four-year-old landscape, thirty metres deep, made of mantle rock that came up in a hurry — and it will look exactly like this long after everyone here is gone.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: Most of the planet is old. This bit is four. Try to be nice to it and please stay off it.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: The Newest Ground In Europe

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: Everything from here to the ridge is younger than the year 2021. **You are about to walk on land that did not exist when you booked your last holiday.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: The **19 March 2021** eruption ran **six months to the day — to 18 September 2021** — and left roughly **150 million cubic metres** of lava across **4.8 km²**, averaging **more than 30 metres thick**, peaking through May and June at around **twelve cubic metres a second.** For scale: that is a new field of rock deeper than a ten-storey building, poured out of a crack in a valley nobody had heard of.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: What makes it strange is what it was made of. Fagradalsfjall's magma is **picrite**, and it came up **fast, and from deep**, without sitting in a shallow chamber first. Most eruptions are fed by magma that has been parked and stewing. This one was mantle material arriving more or less directly. Geologists were, to use the technical term, delighted.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: **The rule for the next two hours: do not walk on the lava.** That is Safetravel's wording. The crust looks solid and is not, the rock is volcanic glass and will open a hand to the bone, and parts of this field are **still warm underneath** years on. Stay on the marked path, and if you want the photo, take it from the path.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: The other rule is the air. **Check the gas dispersal forecast** — geothermal and volcanic ground gives off **sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide**, both heavier than air, both worst in hollows and dips on a still day. **If it smells strongly of eggs in a dip, go up, not on.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall / 🥾 Fagradalsfjall
en: And look at what is growing. Almost nothing — and that is the lesson. There is **no acid rain here, no baking heat, no forest** to break rock down. Iceland barely weathers. **These 2021 flows will still look like this in a thousand years**, which is exactly why the medieval lava we drove over this morning also looks like last week's.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: Iceland pulls about **30% of its electricity** and **90% of its heating** from geothermal. Svartsengi is the textbook made real — and then defended with a digger.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: A power station that accidentally made a spa, then had to be saved by hand from the volcano it lives off.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: The Power Plant That Made The Lagoon

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: That power station accidentally built the Blue Lagoon — and then in 2024 had to be walled off from lava by the metre.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: ***Svartsengi* = Black Meadow**, for the scorched ground it stands on. **Geothermal water from 1976, electricity from 1978 — the first plant anywhere to make both from the same well field.** That first turbine was a modest **1 MW**, quietly running the pumps for its own boreholes.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: It drills **1,000 to 2,000 m** down to water at **240°C**, and now makes **85 MW of electricity** and **190 MW of heat.** The **seventh generating unit came on line on 1 December 2025**, replacing units three and four. That heat is piped across the **Suðurnes**, a region now well over **30,000** people. The **Blue Lagoon** was never planned — just mineral-rich wastewater pooling in the lava next door.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⚡ Svartsengi
en: In **2024**, the eruptions sent lava straight at it. The plant was evacuated and defended with **earthen barriers averaging seven metres**, bulldozed into place in days. **The lava stopped short. It is still running today** — and the same reservoir it drinks from is the one being refilled under our feet right now.

en: ⛰️ Þorbjörn

ctx: cue, tells the guest where to look — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: Look ahead and right — the flat-topped hill standing over the town, with masts on the summit.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: A hill with a collapsed summit, fifteen hanged thieves, an American radar station and a Met Office GPS mast — and it is the last of those that emptied a town.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: Iceland's early-warning system for the biggest evacuation in its modern history was a lump of rock that had already been a hideout, a gallows story and a war station. It just took the promotion.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: Weather pivot: "If Þorbjörn has gone, that is fine — the whole point of this story is that the thing that mattered was never visible anyway. It was two centimetres of ground, and only an instrument could see it."

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: The Mountain That Gave The First Warning

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: On **26 January 2020** the Icelandic Met Office published a sentence it had never been able to write before: in **nearly three decades** of precise measurement, **nothing on this peninsula had ever risen this fast.** That was the first alarm of everything that followed. Grindavík was evacuated **three years, nine months and fifteen days later.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: **Þorbjörn** — properly **Þorbjarnarfell** — is **243 metres**, and it is **móberg**, built underneath ice like Sveifluháls this morning. But this one took **two separate glacial periods** to finish, which makes it **one of the older hills on the peninsula** — considerably older than Fagradalsfjall, where we were standing at eleven o'clock. Look at the top: it has **fallen in on itself.** There is a fault and a small rift valley up there, and — this is the odd part — **that fault runs north to south, straight across the south-west-to-north-east grain of every other crack on Reykjanes.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: The cleft splitting the summit is **Þjófagjá**, Thieves' Gorge, and *Huld* — the nineteenth-century folk collection — says **fifteen thieves** once lived in it, robbing Grindavík's sheep. Nobody could get at them. Then a farmer's son from **Hóp** noticed they all bathed at **Baðsvellir** every Saturday, taking turns guarding the clothes. Once they trusted him with the pile, **he turned one shirt-sleeve and one trouser-leg inside out on every single set**, and ran. They lost the race getting dressed, chased him across the lava in their underwear, cut their feet to ribbons, and were caught and hanged at **Gálgaklettar** — Gallows Rocks. The story ends with one of the great Icelandic shrugs: ***"the farmer's son became an unlucky man, but it is not recorded what befell him."***

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: There was a war up there too. **Camp Vail** was a **United States Army Air Forces radar station** — American, not British, and guides get that wrong. The road up the mountain was begun in **early October 1941** by an air-force construction unit working alongside **men hired in Grindavík**, and the station went live on **18 April 1942**: **fourteen Nissen huts** and a generator, down in the crater, with the radar on the summit. It was **the best station in the country for spotting low-flying aircraft over Faxaflói** — and it was **usable only 60% of the time**, because the antenna had to be folded down that often in the wind. Most of it was sold or demolished after the war. **A single stone hearth is still standing up there.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: Now the part that matters. On **21 January 2020** the ground started rising — **3 to 4 millimetres a day**, about **two centimetres** by the time it was announced on the **26th**. Say this next bit accurately, because almost everyone says it wrong: **the centre of the uplift was not under Þorbjörn. It was just west of it.** Underneath, roughly **a million cubic metres of magma at three to five kilometres down.** On the **22nd**, two earthquakes of **magnitude 3.7 and 3.6** were felt as far north as **Borgarnes.** At **17:19 on the 26th**, the National Commissioner declared an **óvissustig** — an uncertainty phase. That was the first alert level of this entire volcanic episode.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: And then nothing happened, for years. The uplift came and went in pulses. That alert stayed in force. **On the night of 10 November 2023, at 23:48, Grindavík was evacuated** — and the eruptions we have been talking about all day began. **The warning arrived first, and it arrived from this hill.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: Two footnotes. There is a **GPS station on that summit, code THOB**, and Benedikt Ófeigsson of the Met Office **installed it at dusk at the end of January 2020** — put there because of exactly this. And note the language has moved on: **the Met Office no longer calls it the Þorbjörn signal. Every bulletin now says Svartsengi.** *(The masts you can actually see up there are telephone and aviation kit, not science. The instrument that matters is small and you cannot see it from here.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Fagradalsfjall → Grindavík / ⛰️ Þorbjörn
en: One thing under the wheels. The barriers protecting the town and the power plant now run **13.5 kilometres**, hold about **2.5 million cubic metres** of material — the engineers at Verkís cheerfully put that at **"more than a hundred Hallgrímskirkjas"** — and stand **seven metres on average, twenty-four at the highest point.** They cost the country around **seven billion krónur**, under a law Alþingi passed on **13 November 2023, three days after the evacuation.** And **one of them crosses this road.** *(This tarmac is also newer than most of the guests: **Suðurstrandarvegur opened on 21 June 2012** — 57 kilometres to Þorlákshöfn. The road it replaced had been in service since 1946.)*

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: The Town That Came Back

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: This town stood for a thousand years. On **10 November 2023** the ground tore open beneath it in a single night — and every single person got out. **Then 874 of them moved back in.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: **Grindavík** was settled around **934 CE** — one of the first Reykjanes communities and a major North Atlantic **cod harbour.** By December 2023 it held about **3,720 people.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: On **10 November 2023**, thousands of earthquakes in a few hours drove a **dike roughly 15 kilometres long** under the town. Fissures **metres wide** opened through roads, gardens and house foundations, the ground **subsided about a metre** and **pulled apart by around 120 centimetres.** The whole town was **evacuated in one night.** In **January 2024**, lava reached the streets for the first time — houses burned, roads buried.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: Further eruptions followed through 2024 and into 2025 as the **Sundhnúkur crater row** kept reactivating. **Earthen barriers built in days** — six to ten metres by design, twenty-four at the highest point — saved some streets and were overrun on others. For all that, **none of this lava ever reached the sea.** It crossed the Grindavíkurvegur road again and again and pushed into the town on **14 January 2024**, but it never made the coast. The last time lava ran into the sea on this peninsula was the **twelfth century.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: And then people started coming back. The state buyout company **Þórkatla** bought **over 90% of the homes**, and most residents did leave for good — but at **1 April 2026** Þjóðskrá had **874 registered residents** living here again. The **school is open** for the autumn term, the **library** has been brought back to its feet, and the **harbour and the power plant never stopped at all.** In **April 2026** Alþingi debated a formal framework for rebuilding the community. *(Not a ghost town. A very small town with an extremely dramatic CV.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: **Say this bit out loud, because it changes how people behave:** the ground here is still moving and **crevasses are still opening.** That is why we stay on made surfaces and off verges, gardens and shortcuts. People live here. They did not survive all that to have a coach party fall down a hole in their street.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík / 🌋 Grindavík
en: One older raid, because this harbour has form. On **20 June 1627** corsairs out of **Salé** in Morocco under **Murat Reis** took **12 to 15 Icelanders** from Grindavík, along with Danish and Dutch crew, and sailed them to **Algiers** — the opening act of the **Tyrkjaránið**, the Turkish Raid. Of everyone seized around Iceland that summer, **only 27** ever made it home, **nine years later.**

en: Grindavík was never one town. It was **three villages**, and this is the one that **lost.** There is a golf course on it now, and underneath the fairways are a **Danish customs post**, a **churchyard in use since about the year 1200**, and iron **mooring bolts** for tying up sailing ships.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: The three *hverfi* were **Þórkötlustaðahverfi** in the east, **Járngerðarstaðahverfi** in the middle — that is modern Grindavík — and **Staðarhverfi**, here in the west. The middle one won because it had the better landing, and because **the area's first shop opened there around 1900.** Grindavík got its town charter in **1947.** Staðarhverfi just quietly emptied: the parsonage at **Staður** lasted until **1928**, the farm at **Húsatóftir** to about **1946**, and **Staður** itself to around **1964.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: There has been a **church at Staður since at least about 1200** — it is in Bishop Páll Jónsson's church register. It was abolished on **26 September 1909**, the day the new church at Járngerðarstaðir was consecrated. But look again: **the graveyard is still the burial ground for the whole parish.** The town moved. The dead stayed.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: In the bell-gate hangs a bell reading **"SS. Anlaby 1898 Hull."** It is the ship's bell of a Hull trawler that went onto the rocks here on the night of **14 January 1902** and was **lost with all hands.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: This was also, for eighty years, **where Iceland traded with Denmark.** The 1602 monopoly assigned Grindavík harbour to **Copenhagen.** Merchants stopped coming in **1639**, resumed in **1665** with booths at **Arfadalsvík** right here, put up a proper trading house in **1731** — and then in **1745 simply stopped sailing**, blaming sand ruining the harbour. Free trade came in **1787**, the buyer went bankrupt in **1796**, and the buildings were **pulled down in 1806.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: You can still see how they moored. There is an iron bolt in **Bindisker** on one side of the bay and another in **Barlestarsker** on the other, and a **chain was run between them** to lash the trading ships down. The bolt has been **legally protected since 1930.** *(There is a protected national monument in the rough.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: The name is the joke. **Húsatóftir** means **"the house-ruins"** — because after the merchants left, somebody built a farm **inside the foundations of their warehouses.** The golf club was founded on **14 May 1981** and the clubhouse is a **1930 farmhouse.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / ⛳ Staðarhverfi & Húsatóftir
en: And settle one thing before anyone asks: **the 1627 corsair raid did not happen here.** In 1627 the trade — and the ships — were still at Járngerðarstaðir. The merchants only moved west **thirty-eight years later.**

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: The Beach That Played Iwo Jima

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: In the summer of **2005**, **Clint Eastwood** brought a film unit to that beach and shot most of *Flags of Our Fathers* on it. **Iceland played a Pacific island.** And this morning's stop — Krýsuvík — was the second location.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: The reason is the sand. They started scouting in **Hawaii** and it did not work. The location manager, **Kokayi Ampah**, put it bluntly: the beaches were not long or wide enough, and *"it was very tropical — it didn't fit the look of Iwo Jima after it had been pounded by bombshells for a month."* Iwo Jima itself was out of the question — it is a war grave.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: So he went looking for black sand at scale, and Eastwood's own line about flying in was: *"Flying in over the black sand beaches and lava fields, I could see that Iceland had the rugged and unusual look we needed."*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: The detail that makes the whole thing work: the Marines in the film have to **climb a slope of loose black sand that gives way under them.** That is not choreography. That is what this beach does, and it is exactly what the real beach did in 1945.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: Practical Icelandic footnote: the production chartered **two Icelandic Coast Guard vessels** for the landing shots at **a million krónur a day**, and hired **several hundred Icelandic extras**, organised into platoons. And **Mount Suribachi is not there** — the mountain in the film is entirely computer-generated.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🎬 Sandvík
en: The other thing on this shore, and you can walk it: the **Bridge Between Continents**, a footbridge over a rift fissure — which we will come to properly at the lighthouse.

en: Drinking From The Ridge

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🔌 Reykjanesvirkjun
en: The plant we are passing started up in May 2006. Within months the ground at our next stop began to boil harder, swallowed its own car park, and had to be rebuilt.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🔌 Reykjanesvirkjun
en: **HS Orka's Reykjanes power plant** began producing electricity in **May 2006** with **two 50 MW turbines.** Today it runs at **130 MW of installed capacity**, fed by **28 wells** with something like **55 kilometres of drilling** between them. This is the ridge itself being tapped — the hottest, most direct geothermal resource on the peninsula.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🔌 Reykjanesvirkjun
en: And there was a consequence nobody sold tickets for. As **pressure in the reservoir drew down**, steaming at the surface **increased markedly** at **Gunnuhver**, a few hundred metres away. The field surged and grew. It **destroyed the access road and the old walking platforms.** By **2008** field reports describe a **brand-new mud spring about eight metres across, flinging mud four metres into the air**, and steam rising halfway up the slopes of **Skálafell.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Grindavík → Gunnuhver / 🔌 Reykjanesvirkjun
en: New boardwalks and viewing platforms — with universal access — were **completed by summer 2010.** So when we get out in a minute and I tell you to stay on the boards, understand that the boards themselves are the second attempt.

en: The Ghost They Paid Eight Bottles To Move

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: This is where the peninsula stops pretending to be solid ground. And it is named after a woman who was **so angry about a stolen cooking pot** that it took a sorcerer-priest, a ball of yarn and eight bottles of brennivín to get rid of her.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: The headline act, on the official site panels, is **Iceland's largest mud pool — about 20 metres across**, boiling behind a rim of grey mud, with steam columns you can spot from far down the road. Around it the ground has been cooked into reds, yellows and whites, and the soundtrack is pure percussion — plops, hisses, and the occasional full-throated roar.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: The recipe is the same as Seltún's and just as vicious. **Steam rises off the deep reservoir, condenses near the surface, and carries carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide with it.** Those gases turn the water acid, and the acid **digests fresh lava into soft clay.** Everything you are photographing is bedrock that has been dissolved.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: Now the ghost. The name means **Gunna's hot spring**, and Gunna — properly **Guðrún Önundardóttir** — earned it the hard way, about **four hundred years ago** by the legend preserved in **Jón Árnason's** great folk-tale collection. She was a poor woman on the Suðurnes who fell behind on a debt to a man called **Vilhjálmur**, and he confiscated the one thing she could not spare: **her cooking pot.** She died soon after, absolutely furious, and stayed that way.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: At the funeral **her coffin turned suspiciously light**, and people swore they heard her say there was no need to dig deep, as she did not plan to lie there long. She kept her word. Vilhjálmur was found dead in a hollow, badly battered, and the hauntings escalated until Gunna was **riding rooftops** and terrorising people and livestock alike.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: Salvation arrived in liquid form. Two men rode to **Eiríkur Magnússon**, the sorcerer-priest at **Vogsósar**, who agreed to help **for a fee of eight bottles of brennivín.** He handed over a **ball of yarn** with instructions to get Gunna to grab the loose end. When she did, she snapped that she had expected **the Devil himself, not the old man of Vogsósar.** The ball rolled, Gunna followed, and at the hot spring she circled until the yarn ran out — **then plunged in. She has been steaming about it ever since.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Gunnuhver / 👻 Gunnuhver
en: **The current vents largely took shape after an earthquake swarm in 1967**, and then reorganised themselves again after **2006**, as we just discussed. Off the boardwalk the crust can be **a thin lid over boiling acid clay.** Stay on the platforms, keep children by the hand, and let the steam come to you.

en: The Lighthouse The Ground Tried To Evict

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: Most countries build a lighthouse to warn ships about the dangerous bit. Iceland built its first one in 1878 and then discovered **the dangerous bit was the lighthouse.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: **Reykjanesviti is the oldest lighthouse site in Iceland**, and that comes with an asterisk worth explaining. The first tower was lit in **1878** — the country's very first — out on the wind-hammered **Valahnúkur** cliffs. It lasted **eight years** before an earthquake in **1887** cracked it up.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: By **1905** quakes and surf had chewed the headland so badly that the structure was in real danger of sliding into the sea. Not "might erode eventually" — going to fall in. So a second tower went up on the safer hill of **Bæjarfell** between roughly **1907 and 1908**, and the original was finished off with **explosives on 16 April 1908** — a rare case of a lighthouse being decommissioned by demolition charge rather than a retirement party.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: **Settle the argument for them:** the **site** dates to **1878**. The **tower you are photographing** is the **1907–08** model, with re-illumination cited for **1929**. Both statements are true. The architect was **Frederik Kjørboe**, the engineer **Thorvald Krabbe** — the man who effectively ran Iceland's lighthouse and harbour building for decades.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: On height, **the sources disagree and I am not going to tidy it up for you** — some list the tower at about **26 metres** with the light **69 metres** above the sea, others give **31** and **73**. Either way the trick is the one every Icelander learns eventually: **you do not need to build tall if you build on a hill.** The light throws a **double flash every 30 seconds** as the landfall guide for ships steering toward Reykjavík and Keflavík. The country's front-door light, left on for the neighbours.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: Walk the other way and you reach the **Bridge Between Continents**, a footbridge over a sandy rift. Cross it and you have — in the brochure version — walked from North America to Eurasia. Geologists will concede the point politely, note that the plates really are separating **at roughly the speed your fingernails grow**, and then remind you the real boundary is a **messy zone, not one photogenic gap.** The image still holds: the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge spends almost all of its 16,000 kilometres hidden under the ocean**, and here it climbs into the daylight.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🗼 Reykjanesviti
en: Icelanders voted this **the most popular lighthouse in the country in a 2007 survey.** We do love a stubborn thing that refuses to fall down.

en: A bird that could not fly, on an island nobody could reach without ropes, hunted to the last two by three men in a rowing boat working to a collector's order — in **1844**, within the lifetime of people whose grandchildren owned cameras.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: The gannets out there are thriving — nearly fifteen thousand pairs of them. The auks are a statue. Same rock. That is the whole lesson, and it does not need a speech from me.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: The Rock Where A Species Ended

ctx: opening hook line — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: On that rock, in the **first days of June 1844**, two men each killed a bird, a third came back empty-handed, and **the great auk ceased to exist.** Not "became rare." **Ended.** You are looking at the exact place.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: **Eldey** is a **77-metre** sheer-sided cliff island about **15 kilometres** offshore. It holds **14,810 nesting pairs of gannets** — that is the last published count, from **2013–14** — which is **39.8% of every gannet in Iceland.** Be careful with the superlative: it is **Iceland's largest** gannet colony and **one of the world's largest.** The biggest are in the British Isles.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: It has been protected since **1940**, by a law written specifically for it — **the first bird reserve in Iceland.** Declared a *friðland* in **1960**, re-protected in **1974.** You cannot land without permission, and **you may not fire a gun within two kilometres of it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: Now the auks. Their real stronghold was **Geirfuglasker** — Great Auk Skerry — further out. On **6 or 7 March 1830** a submarine eruption began and **destroyed the island.** The survivors moved to Eldey, onto a ledge called **Undirlendið**. In the summer of **1834** two brothers took **thirteen** of them off that ledge and sold them to merchants in Keflavík and Reykjavík. Then it was one or two at a time.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: The last hunt was commissioned by a **collector in Copenhagen** who wanted specimens. Three men climbed Eldey: **Jón Brandsson**, **Sigurður Ísleifsson** and **Ketill Ketilsson.** Jón and Sigurður each caught and strangled a bird. Ketill found nothing, because there was nothing left to find. **The egg the pair were sitting on was broken and thrown away.** The birds' internal organs are still in the natural history museum in **Copenhagen**, catalogued.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 14.0 / Reykjanesviti & the coast / 🐧 Eldey & The Great Auk
en: **On the date, be precise, because half the internet is wrong.** The traditional date is **3 June 1844.** The most recent peer-reviewed work narrows it only to **between the 2nd and the 5th of June 1844.** The University of Iceland's own science service says simply "early June." *(A United Nations page says 3 July. It is wrong. Do not repeat it.)*
